name: Learn: Modify Existing Assets (tricky bits)
objective: CKAD exam-reality: questions hand you assets that ALREADY exist and ask you to change them. Goal: handle the non-obvious immutability quirks — relabel a Deployment (immutable selector), change a bare Pod (immutable in place), edit an on-disk manifest and re-apply, and make running pods pick up a changed ConfigMap.
description: Four pre-seeded assets in 'modify-learn', each needing a change that isn't a straight edit: an immutable Deployment selector, an immutable Pod, an on-disk YAML you must edit + apply, and a ConfigMap whose change only lands after a rollout restart.

questions.title: Relabel a Deployment (selector is immutable)
questions.teach:
A Deployment's `.spec.selector` is **immutable**, so you can't edit it in place to relabel. Instead dump it to YAML, change both the selector and the matching pod-template labels, and recreate with `kubectl replace --force -f` (delete+recreate in one command).

**Gotcha:** the pod-template labels must always match the selector — change both together or the API rejects it.
questions.prompt:
The Deployment `legacy` in `modify-learn` has selector and pod labels `app=legacy`. Relabel it so both its selector and its pods use `app=payments` instead.

Target: Deployment `legacy` exists with `.spec.selector.matchLabels.app=payments`, matching pod-template labels, and at least one available replica.
questions.hint: You can't edit the selector in place (it's immutable). Recreate: `kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o yaml > /tmp/legacy.yaml`, change every `app: legacy` to `app: payments`, then `kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/legacy.yaml`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o yaml > /tmp/legacy.yaml
sed -i '' 's/app: legacy/app: payments/g' /tmp/legacy.yaml   # (Linux: sed -i 's/.../g')
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/legacy.yaml
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o wide

verification.description: legacy recreated with selector+pods relabeled app=payments

questions.eli5:
A Deployment uses a **`selector`** to recognize its own Pods — think of it as a **wristband colour** at an event. The Deployment hands out blue wristbands (`app=legacy`) and says "I only manage people wearing blue." The trouble: once the event starts, **the wristband colour is set in stone**. You can't change "blue" to "green" on a live Deployment — Kubernetes rejects it, because mid-event it would suddenly lose track of everyone wearing blue.

So to truly relabel from `app=legacy` to `app=payments`, you can't edit in place. You have to **tear down the whole setup and rebuild it** with the new colour baked in from the start. The clean one-liner for that is `kubectl replace --force -f file.yaml` — it deletes the old Deployment and creates the new one in a single step.

The other critical rule: the **selector** and the **pod-template labels must always match**. The Deployment only adopts Pods whose labels match its selector. Change one but not the other and the API throws it out immediately.

```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o yaml > /tmp/legacy.yaml
sed -i '' 's/app: legacy/app: payments/g' /tmp/legacy.yaml   # Linux: sed -i '...'
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/legacy.yaml
```

**Watch out for:**

- **`.spec.selector` is immutable.** A plain `kubectl edit` to change it will be rejected. You must recreate.
- **Change BOTH places together** — the selector *and* the pod-template `labels`. Mismatched → API error.
- **`replace --force` deletes then recreates** — there's a brief moment with no Pods. Fine for a lab; be careful in production.
- **`sed` differs by OS**: macOS needs `sed -i ''`, Linux needs `sed -i`. The exam runs Linux.
- Don't miss a stray `app: legacy` (e.g. in `metadata.labels`) — `g` replaces all, but check.
questions.deepDive:
## Relabel a Deployment (selector is immutable) — full rundown

### Mental model
A Deployment's `.spec.selector.matchLabels` is how it **claims** its ReplicaSet/Pods. To keep that relationship stable, Kubernetes makes the **selector immutable after creation**. You therefore cannot `edit`/`apply` a new selector onto a live Deployment — you must **delete and recreate** it with the new labels, keeping selector and pod-template labels in sync.

### The invariant
```
spec.selector.matchLabels  ⊆  spec.template.metadata.labels
```
The pod template's labels must be a **superset of (match)** the selector. Break this and the API rejects the object:
```
selector does not match template labels
```

### What you cannot do
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn edit deployment legacy      # change selector -> REJECTED
# The Deployment "legacy" is invalid: spec.selector: Invalid value:
#   field is immutable
kubectl -n modify-learn apply -f new.yaml            # also rejected for selector change
```

### The fix — dump, edit both, replace --force
```bash
# 1. dump current object
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o yaml > /tmp/legacy.yaml

# 2. change EVERY app: legacy  ->  app: payments  (selector AND template labels)
sed -i 's/app: legacy/app: payments/g' /tmp/legacy.yaml      # Linux (exam)
# macOS: sed -i '' 's/app: legacy/app: payments/g' /tmp/legacy.yaml

# 3. delete + recreate in one command
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/legacy.yaml

# 4. verify
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o wide
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.selector.matchLabels.app}'; echo    # payments
```

### Where `app: legacy` appears in a dumped Deployment
| Location | Must change? |
|---|---|
| `spec.selector.matchLabels.app` | ✅ yes (the whole point) |
| `spec.template.metadata.labels.app` | ✅ yes (must match selector) |
| `metadata.labels.app` (Deployment's own) | optional, but `g` catches it |
| `metadata.labels` on the Service selecting it | change separately if a Service targets it |

### `replace --force` vs alternatives
| Command | Behaviour | Selector change? |
|---|---|---|
| `kubectl edit` | in-place PATCH | ❌ rejected |
| `kubectl apply` | 3-way merge PATCH | ❌ rejected |
| `kubectl replace -f` | full PUT (no delete) | ❌ still rejected (immutable) |
| `kubectl replace --force -f` | **delete + create** | ✅ works |
| `kubectl delete` then `create -f` | two steps, same effect | ✅ works |

`--force` is what makes `replace` do a delete+recreate rather than a PUT.

### Cleaning server-managed fields (optional)
A raw `get -o yaml` dump includes `status`, `resourceVersion`, `uid`, `creationTimestamp`. `replace --force` tolerates these (it recreates), but for `create -f` you'd strip them. For speed on the exam, `replace --force` just works.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Selector is immutable** — never try to edit it in place; recreate.
- **Change selector AND template labels together** — a mismatch is a hard API error.
- **`replace --force` = delete + create** → brief downtime; acceptable in a lab, risky in prod (use a new Deployment + traffic shift there).
- **`sed -i` syntax differs**: Linux `sed -i 's/.../'`, macOS `sed -i '' 's/.../'`. The exam is Linux.
- Watch for **other objects** (Services, HPAs) that select `app=legacy` — they won't find the relabeled pods until you update their selectors too.
- After recreate, confirm **at least one replica is Available** (`get deploy -o wide`).

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy legacy -o yaml > /tmp/legacy.yaml
sed -i 's/app: legacy/app: payments/g' /tmp/legacy.yaml
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/legacy.yaml
```
Immutable-field rule: **selector can't change in place → delete + recreate.**

questions.title: Change a bare Pod (immutable in place)
questions.teach:
A running Pod's `env` can't be changed in place — a bare Pod is almost entirely immutable. To add env, dump it to YAML, add the var under the container, and recreate with `kubectl replace --force -f` (delete+recreate in one step).

**Gotcha:** `kubectl set env pod/<name> …` fails — `set env` works on templates like Deployments, not on live Pods.
questions.prompt:
A bare Pod `tool` (busybox) runs in `modify-learn`. Add an environment variable `MODE=prod` to its container.

Target: Pod `tool` is Running and its container has env `MODE=prod`.
questions.hint: You can't add env to a live Pod (`set env pod/...` and `edit` are rejected). Recreate it: `kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o yaml > /tmp/tool.yaml`, add the env under the container, then `kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/tool.yaml`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o yaml > /tmp/tool.yaml
# add under containers[0]:  env: [{name: MODE, value: prod}]
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/tool.yaml
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].env}'

verification.description: pod tool recreated with env MODE=prod

questions.eli5:
A bare **Pod** is like a cake that's **already baked**. You can't stir in another egg after it's out of the oven — most of its ingredients (like environment variables) are locked once it's running. A Deployment is more like a *recipe* you can keep tweaking, but a lone Pod is the finished cake.

So when the task says "add env `MODE=prod` to the Pod `tool`," you can't just reach in and change it. `kubectl set env pod/tool MODE=prod` **fails** — `set env` works on templates (Deployments, etc.), not on a live Pod. `kubectl edit pod/tool` won't let you add env either.

The move is the same pattern as the immutable Deployment selector: **bake a new cake.** Dump the Pod to YAML, add the env var under its container, then recreate with `kubectl replace --force -f` (delete + create in one step).

```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o yaml > /tmp/tool.yaml
# add under containers[0]:   env: [{name: MODE, value: prod}]
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/tool.yaml
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].env}'
```

**Watch out for:**

- **`kubectl set env pod/<name>` fails** — it only edits controller templates, not live Pods.
- **`kubectl edit pod` can't add env** either — the container env list is immutable on a running Pod.
- **`replace --force` deletes then recreates** the Pod — it gets a new start, new IP, resets its uptime. That's expected and necessary here.
- **Add env in the right spot** — under the specific container in `spec.containers`, not at the Pod level (there's no Pod-level env).
- **Strip nothing you don't have to** — `replace --force` recreates, so leftover `status`/`resourceVersion` fields are tolerated.
questions.deepDive:
## Change a bare Pod (immutable in place) — full rundown

### Mental model
A **bare Pod** (not managed by a controller) is almost entirely **immutable** after creation. A running Pod's container `env`, image (mostly), volumes, and most spec fields cannot be changed in place — the API server rejects the PATCH. To change them you **recreate** the Pod from an edited manifest.

### What is / isn't mutable on a live Pod
| Field | Mutable in place? |
|---|---|
| container `env` | ❌ no |
| container `image` | ⚠️ limited — only via a rolling/`set image` on controllers; on a bare Pod effectively no |
| `spec.containers[].resources` | ❌ no (except in-place resize alpha/beta) |
| `metadata.labels` / `annotations` | ✅ yes |
| `spec.activeDeadlineSeconds` | ✅ (can only decrease) |
| `spec.tolerations` | ✅ add-only |
| `spec.containers` list / command | ❌ no |

Env sits in the immutable set → recreate.

### Why `set env` / `edit` fail
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn set env pod/tool MODE=prod
# error: cannot set env on a Pod — set env patches a pod *template*
#        (Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet/Job), not a live Pod
kubectl -n modify-learn edit pod tool
# save fails: spec: Forbidden: pod updates may not change fields other than ...
```
`kubectl set env` only targets objects with a pod **template**. A Pod has no template — it *is* the pod — so there's nothing for `set env` to patch.

### The fix — dump, edit, replace --force
```bash
# 1. dump
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o yaml > /tmp/tool.yaml

# 2. add env under the container (containers[0])
#    env:
#    - name: MODE
#      value: prod

# 3. delete + recreate
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/tool.yaml

# 4. verify
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].env}'; echo
# [{"name":"MODE","value":"prod"}]
```

### Where env goes (YAML)
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: tool
    image: busybox:1.36
    env:
    - name: MODE
      value: prod
```
Env is **per-container**; there is no Pod-level `env`.

### Recreate commands compared
| Command | Effect on a bare Pod |
|---|---|
| `kubectl set env pod/tool ...` | ❌ errors (no template) |
| `kubectl edit pod tool` | ❌ rejects env change |
| `kubectl apply -f tool.yaml` | ❌ rejects immutable field change |
| `kubectl replace --force -f tool.yaml` | ✅ delete + recreate |
| `kubectl delete pod tool` then `create -f` | ✅ equivalent, two steps |

### Consequences of recreating
- New Pod UID, new IP, restarted uptime, counters reset.
- Any `status`/`resourceVersion` left in the dumped YAML is fine — `replace --force` recreates from scratch.
- If the Pod was part of a Service's endpoints, it re-registers on restart.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **`set env` does not work on Pods** — only on controllers with a pod template.
- **`edit`/`apply` reject env changes** on a live Pod — immutable.
- **`replace --force` = delete + recreate** — the Pod is genuinely replaced; expect a new IP and reset state.
- Put env under the **correct container**, not at Pod level.
- If the Pod is actually owned by a controller (ReplicaSet), fix the **controller's template** instead — but here it's a bare Pod.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get pod tool -o yaml > /tmp/tool.yaml
# add  env: [{name: MODE, value: prod}]  under containers[0]
kubectl -n modify-learn replace --force -f /tmp/tool.yaml
```
Rule: **bare Pod env is immutable → dump, edit, `replace --force`.**

questions.title: Edit an on-disk manifest and re-apply
questions.teach:
When the asset is a **YAML file on disk** already applied to the cluster, edit the file and re-apply with `kubectl apply -f file.yaml` — the file stays the source of truth. Preview changes first with `kubectl diff -f file.yaml`.

**Gotcha:** `kubectl edit` changes the *live* object but not your file, so the two drift apart — edit the file when a file is the asset.
questions.prompt:
The manifest `/tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml` defines Deployment `widget` (applied at 1 replica, `nginx:1.25`). Edit the **file** to scale it to `3` replicas and update the image to `nginx:1.26`, then apply it.

Target: Deployment `widget` in `modify-learn` has 3 available replicas on image `nginx:1.26`.
questions.hint: Edit `/tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml` (set `replicas: 3` and `image: nginx:1.26`), preview with `kubectl diff -f /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml`, then `kubectl apply -f /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml`.
questions.solution:
sed -i '' -e 's/replicas: 1/replicas: 3/' -e 's/nginx:1.25/nginx:1.26/' /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml
kubectl diff -f /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml
kubectl apply -f /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/widget

verification.description: widget updated to 3 replicas + nginx:1.26 via the on-disk file

questions.eli5:
Sometimes the "thing you're asked to change" isn't the live object in the cluster — it's a **YAML file sitting on disk** that someone already applied. Think of the file as the **master blueprint** and the cluster as the **building built from it**. The right way to remodel is to **edit the blueprint and re-submit it**, so the two stay in agreement. If you instead walk into the building and move walls directly (editing the live object), the blueprint and the building drift apart — next time someone re-applies the old blueprint, your changes vanish.

So here: open `/tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml`, change `replicas: 1` to `3` and the image `nginx:1.25` to `nginx:1.26`, then re-apply the file.

A nice habit: **preview before you commit** with `kubectl diff -f file.yaml` — it shows exactly what will change in the cluster, like a "before/after" of the remodel.

```bash
sed -i '' -e 's/replicas: 1/replicas: 3/' -e 's/nginx:1.25/nginx:1.26/' /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml
kubectl diff -f /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml
kubectl apply -f /tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/widget
```

**Watch out for:**

- **`kubectl edit` changes the *live* object, not your file** — the file and cluster drift. When a file is the asset, edit the **file**.
- **`apply` is the right verb** here (it merges your file into the live object and records it as the source of truth).
- **Image bump = a new rollout.** New Pods on `nginx:1.26` replace the old ones; wait for `rollout status` to confirm all 3 are up.
- **Match the exact strings** — `nginx:1.25` vs `nginx:1.26`; a typo in the tag means the image never updates (or won't pull).
- **`sed -i` syntax differs by OS** — macOS `sed -i ''`, Linux `sed -i`. The exam is Linux.
questions.deepDive:
## Edit an on-disk manifest and re-apply — full rundown

### Mental model
When the asset **is a YAML file** that was applied with `kubectl apply`, the file is the **source of truth**. The correct workflow is **edit the file → preview → re-apply**. `kubectl apply` records the file in a `last-applied-configuration` annotation and performs a **3-way merge**, so re-applying keeps the file and the live object aligned. Editing the live object instead (`kubectl edit`/`scale`) causes **config drift**.

### The workflow
```bash
FILE=/tmp/kindlab-assets/widget-deploy.yaml

# 1. edit the file (replicas 1->3, image 1.25->1.26)
sed -i -e 's/replicas: 1/replicas: 3/' -e 's/nginx:1.25/nginx:1.26/' "$FILE"   # Linux
# macOS: sed -i '' -e '...'

# 2. preview the change against the cluster
kubectl diff -f "$FILE"

# 3. apply
kubectl apply -f "$FILE"

# 4. wait for the rollout
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/widget
```

### `apply` vs `edit` vs `create` vs `replace`
| Command | Operates on | Keeps file in sync? | Records last-applied? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kubectl apply -f` | file → live (3-way merge) | ✅ yes | ✅ yes |
| `kubectl edit` | live object only | ❌ file drifts | n/a |
| `kubectl scale` / `set image` | live object only | ❌ file drifts | n/a |
| `kubectl create -f` | file → live (fails if exists) | n/a | ❌ no |
| `kubectl replace -f` | file → live (full PUT) | ✅ yes | ❌ no annotation |

Use **apply** when a file is the declared asset.

### `kubectl diff`
```bash
kubectl diff -f "$FILE"
# shows a unified diff of live vs the file — exactly what apply would change.
# exit code 1 means "differences exist" (not an error).
```
Great for sanity-checking before mutating the cluster.

### What each change does
| Change | Field | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `replicas: 3` | `spec.replicas` | Deployment scales to 3 Pods |
| `image: nginx:1.26` | `spec.template.spec.containers[].image` | **template change → rolling update**; new ReplicaSet, Pods replaced |

A `replicas` change alone just scales. An **image** change alters the pod template → triggers a rollout (new ReplicaSet), which you watch with `rollout status`.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy widget -o wide
# READY 3/3, IMAGES nginx:1.26
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy widget \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.replicas} {.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'; echo
# 3 nginx:1.26
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Edit the FILE, not the live object.** `kubectl edit`/`scale` change the cluster but leave the file stale → drift, and a later `apply` of the old file reverts you.
- **Use `apply`** (not `create` — object exists; not `replace` unless you intend a full PUT).
- **Image bump = rollout.** Confirm with `rollout status`; don't assume it's instant.
- **Exact image tag** — `nginx:1.26` must match; a wrong tag won't pull / won't satisfy the grader.
- **`sed -i` OS difference** — Linux `sed -i`, macOS `sed -i ''`. Exam is Linux.
- `kubectl diff` exit code 1 = "there are differences", which is expected, not a failure.

### Quick reference
```bash
sed -i -e 's/replicas: 1/replicas: 3/' -e 's/nginx:1.25/nginx:1.26/' $FILE
kubectl diff -f $FILE
kubectl apply -f $FILE
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/widget
```
Rule: **file is the asset → edit the file, `apply`, don't `edit` the live object.**

questions.title: Make pods pick up a changed ConfigMap
questions.teach:
Env injected from a ConfigMap via `valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` is resolved **once, at pod start**, so editing the ConfigMap doesn't change already-running pods. Update the ConfigMap, then `kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name>` so new pods re-read it.

**Gotcha:** only ConfigMaps mounted as a **volume** update live in the container — `env`/`envFrom` values are frozen until a restart.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `web` in `modify-learn` reads env `COLOR` from ConfigMap `web-config` (currently `blue`). Change the config to `green` and make the **running** pods actually serve `COLOR=green`.

Target: ConfigMap `web-config` has `COLOR=green` AND a running `web` pod reports `COLOR=green` from its environment.
questions.hint: Update the CM then roll the pods: `kubectl -n modify-learn create configmap web-config --from-literal=COLOR=green --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -`, then `kubectl -n modify-learn rollout restart deployment/web`. Verify with `kubectl -n modify-learn exec <web-pod> -- printenv COLOR`.
questions.solution:
kubectl -n modify-learn create configmap web-config --from-literal=COLOR=green --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn exec deploy/web -- printenv COLOR   # green

verification.description: web-config=green AND running web pods serve COLOR=green (needed a restart)

questions.eli5:
Imagine each Pod reads its settings off a **printed note** when it's born, then memorizes them and never looks at the note again. The ConfigMap is a whiteboard; when a Pod starts, it **copies** the value `COLOR=blue` onto its own note and walks off. Now you rub out `blue` and write `green` on the whiteboard — but the Pods that already left are still holding notes that say `blue`. They don't check the whiteboard again.

That's exactly how a ConfigMap injected as an **environment variable** works (`valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` or `envFrom`). The value is read **once, at Pod start**, and frozen. Editing the ConfigMap afterward does **nothing** to running Pods.

So to actually make the pods serve `COLOR=green`, two steps:
1. **Update the ConfigMap** to `green`.
2. **Restart the Pods** so new ones are born and copy the fresh value: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/web`.

```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn create configmap web-config --from-literal=COLOR=green --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn exec deploy/web -- printenv COLOR    # green
```

**Watch out for:**

- **Env from a ConfigMap is frozen at Pod start.** Editing the CM alone never updates running Pods — you MUST restart them.
- **Only ConfigMaps mounted as a VOLUME update live** (and even then with a delay, and the app must re-read the file). `env`/`envFrom` never update without a restart.
- **Use `rollout restart`** — it does a clean rolling replacement. Deleting Pods by hand also works but is cruder.
- **The CM update + the restart are BOTH required** — doing just one fails the task.
- The `create ... --dry-run=client -o yaml | apply -f -` trick safely *updates* an existing ConfigMap without a "already exists" error.
questions.deepDive:
## Make pods pick up a changed ConfigMap — full rundown

### Mental model
How a ConfigMap reaches a container determines whether updates propagate:
- **As env (`valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` / `envFrom`)** → resolved **once at Pod start**, then **frozen**. Changing the CM does **not** affect running Pods. You must **recreate the Pods** (rollout restart) so new Pods re-read it.
- **As a mounted volume (`configMap` volume)** → the kubelet **syncs** the file into the container periodically (up to ~1 minute), so the file updates live — but the **app must re-read the file**; the process won't notice on its own.

This step uses **env**, so: update the CM **and** restart the Deployment.

### Propagation matrix
| Mount style | Live update? | Delay | App must re-read? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `env` → `configMapKeyRef` | ❌ no | needs Pod restart | — |
| `envFrom` → `configMapRef` | ❌ no | needs Pod restart | — |
| `volumeMounts` (configMap volume) | ✅ yes | ~ up to 1 min (sync period) | ✅ yes |
| `subPath` volume mount | ❌ no | not updated | — |

### The fix (env case)
```bash
# 1. update the ConfigMap (idempotent apply — no "already exists" error)
kubectl -n modify-learn create configmap web-config \
  --from-literal=COLOR=green --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

# 2. roll the Deployment so new pods read the new value
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/web

# 3. verify from inside a running pod
kubectl -n modify-learn exec deploy/web -- printenv COLOR    # green
```

### Why the `create --dry-run | apply` idiom
`kubectl create configmap` fails if it already exists. Piping `--dry-run=client -o yaml` into `kubectl apply -f -` **generates** the desired object and **applies** it (create-or-update), avoiding the conflict. Equivalent alternatives:
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn edit configmap web-config          # change COLOR: green
kubectl -n modify-learn patch configmap web-config -p '{"data":{"COLOR":"green"}}'
```

### `rollout restart` — what it does
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout restart deployment/web
```
Adds/updates a `kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt` annotation on the pod template → the Deployment template changes → a normal **rolling update** replaces every Pod. New Pods start and re-evaluate their env from the current ConfigMap. (Deleting Pods manually works too but isn't graceful/rolling.)

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Env values are frozen at start** — editing the CM alone does nothing to running Pods. The restart is mandatory.
- **Volume-mounted CMs update live** (with delay) — but `env`/`envFrom` never do. Know which style the Pod uses.
- **`subPath` volume mounts do NOT get live updates** even though they're volumes — a classic trap.
- **Both actions required**: update CM *and* restart. The grader checks CM=green **and** a running pod reporting green.
- `rollout restart` is the clean way; raw `kubectl delete pod` also forces a re-read but skips rolling safety.
- After restart, verify with `exec ... printenv` on a **new** pod, not a cached one.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn create configmap web-config \
  --from-literal=COLOR=green --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout restart deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn rollout status deployment/web
kubectl -n modify-learn exec deploy/web -- printenv COLOR
```
Rule: **ConfigMap-as-env is frozen at start → update CM + `rollout restart`.**

questions.title: Rename a container without ending up with two
questions.teach:
`kubectl apply` merges the `containers` list by `name`. Renaming a container on a Deployment that has no `last-applied` annotation (created with `kubectl create`/`run`) does a 2-way merge — it **adds** the new name and **keeps** the old, leaving TWO containers. Rename cleanly with `kubectl edit`, `kubectl replace -f`, or a JSON patch instead.

**Gotcha:** 'nothing changed' after apply usually means you now have both containers — check `kubectl get deploy -o jsonpath='{..containers[*].name}'`.

Target: `renamer` has exactly ONE container, named `web`, image `nginx:1.25`.

Use `kubectl -n modify-learn edit deployment renamer` (change the name), or a JSON patch: `kubectl -n modify-learn patch deployment renamer --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/name","value":"web"}]'`.

questions.eli5:
Here's a sneaky one. You want to **rename** a container from `nginx` to `web`. Seems easy — just change the name in a manifest and `kubectl apply`, right? That's the trap.

Think of `kubectl apply` as a librarian who **merges** your updated card into the catalog, matching entries **by name**. When you hand over a card that says the container is now called `web`, the librarian doesn't recognize `web` (there was only `nginx` before), so she **files it as a NEW container** — and keeps the old `nginx` card too. Now your Pod has **two containers**, which is almost never what you wanted.

Why does this happen here specifically? This Deployment was made imperatively (`kubectl create`/`run`), so it has **no "last-applied" memory** for `apply` to compare against. With no memory, `apply` can only do a basic 2-way merge, which *adds* and never *removes* list items.

The clean fix is to change the name **in place** on the live object, where there's no ambiguous merge:

```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn patch deployment renamer --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/name","value":"web"}]'
```

A JSON patch says "replace the name at index 0" — surgical, exactly one container results. `kubectl edit` works too.

**Watch out for:**

- **`apply` of a renamed container leaves TWO containers** (adds new, keeps old) — especially on imperatively-created objects with no last-applied annotation.
- **The telltale sign**: after apply it says "unchanged" or the Pod won't start — check `kubectl get deploy renamer -o jsonpath='{..containers[*].name}'`; if you see two names, that's the bug.
- **Use `edit`, `replace -f`, or a JSON patch** to rename cleanly — never a 2-way `apply`.
- **JSON patch is index-based** (`/containers/0/name`) — make sure index 0 is the right container.
- Target state is **exactly one** container named `web`, image unchanged (`nginx:1.25`).
questions.deepDive:
## Rename a container without ending up with two — full rundown

### Mental model
`kubectl apply` merges the `containers` list **by the `name` key** (it's a "patch strategic merge" keyed list). Renaming a container therefore reads as **"delete the entry named X, add a new entry named Y"** — but a **2-way** merge (no stored `last-applied-configuration`) can only *add* Y; it has no record telling it to *remove* X. Result: **two containers**. Objects created with `kubectl create`/`run` have **no** last-applied annotation, so `apply` falls back to the lossy 2-way merge.

### Why the annotation matters
| Object created by | Has `last-applied` annotation? | `apply` merge type | Rename result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kubectl apply -f` | ✅ yes | 3-way (knows prior desired) | can remove old → one container* |
| `kubectl create` / `kubectl run` | ❌ no | 2-way (only adds) | **two containers** |

\*even with 3-way, renaming lists is fragile; prefer explicit methods.

### The clean fixes
**JSON patch (surgical, index-based):**
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn patch deployment renamer --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/name","value":"web"}]'
```
**Interactive edit:**
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn edit deployment renamer      # change name: nginx -> web
```
**Full replace from a corrected file:**
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy renamer -o yaml > /tmp/r.yaml
sed -i 's/name: nginx/name: web/' /tmp/r.yaml         # (only the container name)
kubectl -n modify-learn replace -f /tmp/r.yaml
```
All three change the name **in place**, producing exactly one container.

### Patch types compared
| `--type` | Semantics | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| (default) strategic merge | merge by list key `name` | add/modify fields; **not** safe for rename |
| `merge` (RFC 7386) | shallow object merge | simple scalar fields |
| `json` (RFC 6902) | op/path operations (`replace`, `remove`, `add`) | **precise list edits like rename** |

For a rename, `--type=json` with `replace` on `/containers/0/name` is the most reliable.

### Detecting the two-container bug
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy renamer \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].name}'; echo
# BAD:  nginx web      (two)
# GOOD: web            (one)
```
Symptoms of the trap: apply reports `configured`/`unchanged` but Pods now have an extra (possibly crashing) container, or the rollout stalls.

### Verify success
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy renamer \
  -o jsonpath='{range .spec.template.spec.containers[*]}{.name}={.image}{"\n"}{end}'
# web=nginx:1.25        (exactly one, image unchanged)
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Naive `apply` of a renamed container keeps BOTH** — the headline trap, worst on imperatively-created objects.
- **List merge is by `name`** — changing `name` is an add, not a rename, to the merge engine.
- **Use `edit` / `replace -f` / JSON patch** to rename; avoid 2-way `apply`.
- **JSON patch paths are index-based** (`/containers/0/...`) — verify the index points at the right container.
- Keep the **image unchanged** — the task renames only; don't accidentally bump the tag.
- If you already created two containers, remove the stray one with a JSON `remove` op or re-`replace` a clean manifest.

### Quick reference
```bash
kubectl -n modify-learn patch deployment renamer --type=json \
  -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/name","value":"web"}]'
kubectl -n modify-learn get deploy renamer \
  -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].name}'   # -> web (one)
```
Rule: **rename ≠ apply. Merge-by-name duplicates → use edit / replace / JSON patch.**
